title: Speed is half the marks — read this first
body:
This is the rule that makes Round 1 unlike any exam you have sat, and most candidates will not have read it.

> **Official wording:** *"You'll get separate marks for accuracy (correct answer) and speed (time taken to answer). Example: A question of 4 marks has a timer of 120 seconds with the correct answer as Unstop. You answered Unstop in 30 seconds. Then you get 2 for accuracy and 1.5 for speed, so a total of 3.5 marks. Marks for speed are calculated based on the percentage of time remaining."*

### The maths

Half the marks are accuracy, half are speed, and speed scales linearly with the fraction of the question's time still on the clock:

```text
marks = (M / 2)                     if correct, else 0
      + (M / 2) x (time_remaining / time_allowed)   for speed
```

With a 60-second question worth 4 marks:

| Answered at | Time remaining | Accuracy | Speed | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 s | 83% | 2.0 | 1.67 | **3.67** |
| 20 s | 67% | 2.0 | 1.33 | **3.33** |
| 30 s | 50% | 2.0 | 1.00 | **3.00** |
| 45 s | 25% | 2.0 | 0.50 | **2.50** |
| 58 s | 3% | 2.0 | 0.07 | **2.07** |

**Answering a question you know in 10 seconds instead of 45 is worth more than a whole extra correct answer's accuracy marks.** Across 15 questions, habitually answering at 20 s rather than 45 s is worth roughly **12 marks** — the difference between shortlisted and not.

### What this changes about how you sit the paper

- **The moment you know it, submit it.** Do not re-read. Do not double-check a question you were confident about. Confirmation costs more than it protects.
- **Never run the clock down.** There is no benefit to using your full minute — you cannot go back, so time not spent answering is simply thrown away.
- **Decide fast on the ones you do not know.** If you are 15 seconds in with no route to the answer, eliminate and commit. Sitting there earns nothing even if you eventually get it right, because speed marks are already gone.

### The one caveat, stated honestly

The guidelines do not explicitly say whether speed marks are awarded on a *wrong* answer. The worked example only covers a correct one. **Assume speed marks require a correct answer** — if it were otherwise, slamming a random option in one second on every question would be optimal, which no assessment is designed to reward. So: fast **and** right. Do not turn this into a reason to guess instantly.
checklist: Submit the instant you are confident — no re-reading
Never let a question's clock run out on a question you can answer
15-second rule on questions you cannot see a route into
Practise on the mock until fast submission feels normal

title: You cannot go back — and what that removes from your toolkit
body:
> **Official wording:** *"You won't be able to browse through the questions. If you either skip your question or submit your answer, it is marked and stored, and cannot be altered."* And: *"You have to submit answers/code/solutions to all the questions individually. Otherwise your response will NOT be recorded."*

**Every exam habit you have built is now wrong.** There is no question palette, no Mark for Review, no two-pass strategy, no coming back at the end. Each question appears once, you answer or skip, and it closes.

### What this deletes

- **The two-pass strategy.** Flagging hard questions to return to later does not exist here. You cannot return.
- **Guessing now and refining later.** Your first submission is your only submission.
- **Banking time for the end.** Time saved on question 3 does not help question 12 — each question has its own minute, and unused time is lost, not pooled.

### What it adds

- **Every question is independent.** A disaster on question 4 cannot bleed into question 5 unless you let it. There is no cumulative time deficit to panic about.
- **The decision is always the same:** answer now, or skip now. That is the entire decision tree. It is simpler than a normal paper, and much less forgiving.

### The forced-commitment routine

1. **Read the last line first** — what is actually being asked.
2. **0–10 s:** do you recognise the pattern? If yes, answer and submit.
3. **10–25 s:** work it, or eliminate options. Commit to whichever gives the best expected value.
4. **25 s:** commit regardless. Pick the best surviving option and submit. Never let the clock expire — an expiry gives you zero speed marks *and* zero chance of the accuracy marks you might have got from an educated guess.

**Never deliberately skip.** Skipping and answering wrongly score the same — zero — but a guess has a real chance of being right. Since there is no negative marking mentioned anywhere in the guidelines, **there is never a reason to leave a question unanswered.** Confirm the negative-marking rule on the instruction screen on the day, but the default assumption is: always answer.
checklist: Unlearn the two-pass habit before the exam, not during it
Commit by 25 seconds on every MCQ
Never let a question auto-expire
Never skip — a guess strictly dominates a blank

title: Section A: 15 MCQs, one minute each
body:
Fifteen questions, sixty seconds each, auto-advance when the minute is up. Sixty seconds is not enough to *derive* an answer. It is enough to *recognise* one.

### The 60-second budget

| Seconds | What should be happening |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Read the last line of the stem. Identify what is being asked. |
| 5–15 | Recognise the pattern. If you know it, answer and submit — you are done at 15 s with 75% of the speed marks. |
| 15–25 | Not recognised: eliminate options. Kill impossible complexity classes, impossible types, impossible magnitudes. |
| 25–40 | Work the survivors. If two remain and you cannot separate them, pick and go. |
| 40 | Hard stop. Submit whatever you have. |

Nothing after 40 seconds is worth much — the speed marks are nearly gone by then and you still risk the auto-advance taking the decision out of your hands.

### Fast elimination heuristics

| Question shape | Fast route |
|---|---|
| Count the loop iterations | Look at where the inner index *starts*. `j = i` → n(n+1)/2. `j = i+1` → n(n-1)/2. `j = 0` → n². |
| "What is the complexity" | Find the loop that multiplies or divides a variable — that is your log. Additive loops do not nest. |
| Predict the output | Look for the trap first: mutation, aliasing, integer division, pre/post increment, short-circuit evaluation. |
| Which data structure | Match the operation set, then the complexity guarantee. "Ordered" rules out hash tables. |
| Which algorithm applies | Look for the disqualifying constraint: negative edges kill Dijkstra, cycles kill topological sort. |
| Normal forms / ACID / isolation | Pure recall. You know it in 10 seconds or you eliminate and move. |
| Probability | Look for the complement — `1 − P(none)` is almost always less arithmetic. |

**Eliminate by dimension.** If the options are `O(n)`, `O(n log n)`, `O(n²)`, `O(2ⁿ)`, a single non-recursive loop can never be exponential, and if nothing halves anything then `O(n log n)` usually dies too. Two eliminations turn a 25% guess into a 50% one, in about four seconds.

**The distractors are built from your mistakes.** In a well-built paper the wrong options are the answers you get by making the specific common error. If your answer appears instantly and exactly as an option, spend three seconds checking you did not fall into the obvious trap — but only three.
checklist: Hard stop and submit at 40 seconds, every question
Practise recognising the seven question shapes above
Eliminate by dimension before working anything
Read the last line of the stem first

title: Section B: 2 coding problems in 45 minutes
body:
The stage description gives Section B 45 minutes for 2 coding challenges — roughly **22 minutes each**, including reading, writing and debugging.

**An ambiguity to resolve on the day.** The guidelines state a blanket *"Time per Question: 00:01:00"* while the stage description gives the coding section 45 minutes. One minute per coding problem would be impossible, so the per-question figure is almost certainly the MCQ section's setting. **Check the actual per-question timer on the first coding screen before you start typing.** If it really shows one minute, your only rational play is to write the most correct skeleton you can in that minute — so know that possibility exists rather than freezing when you see it.

### The 22-minute procedure

| Minutes | What |
|---|---|
| 0–2 | Read fully. Restate the input/output contract in one line. |
| 2–4 | Name the pattern. Two pointers, sliding window, hash counting, sort-then-scan, binary search on the answer, BFS/DFS, topological sort, 1D DP, 2D DP, greedy, monotonic stack, heap. If you cannot name it in two minutes, write the brute force — it often reveals the pattern. |
| 4–6 | Write the signature, the return, and the degenerate cases first. `if not arr: return 0` costs nothing and saves whole test cases. |
| 6–16 | Write the solution. |
| 16–19 | Dry-run sample 1 by hand, tracing the state. This is the highest-value three minutes in the section. |
| 19–22 | Fix, submit. |

**Submitting is final here too.** You cannot come back and improve it, so the calculus changes: **a working brute force submitted beats an elegant solution you are still debugging.** If you have something correct at minute 15 and an optimisation in mind, weigh whether you can finish and verify the optimisation before the clock — if it is close, submit the version that works.

### The bugs that actually cost marks

- **Off-by-one** in loop bounds — `<` vs `<=`, `n-1` vs `n`.
- **Integer overflow in Java and C++.** `int` dies past 2,147,483,647. Constraints allowing values to 10⁹ summed over n elements need `long` / `long long`. Python is immune.
- **Printing instead of returning**, or the reverse. Check what the harness wants.
- **Unhandled empty input.** The suite always includes it.
- **Mutating the input** when the contract forbids it.
- **Reading input wrong** — a parsing bug looks exactly like an algorithm bug and wastes your whole budget.

### Language

Write in whichever you type fastest without lookups. **Python** for fewest keystrokes, no overflow, and `Counter` / `defaultdict` / `deque` / `heapq` / `bisect` / `lru_cache` doing the work. **Java** if you are more fluent there — watch `int` overflow and never `String +=` in a loop. **C++** only if you already compete in it. Decide before the exam, not during.
checklist: Check the real per-question timer on the first coding screen
Restate the contract in one line before coding
Degenerate cases in the first two lines of the function
Dry-run sample 1 by hand before submitting
Submit a working brute force rather than an unfinished optimum

title: Proctoring: set your room up before you start
body:
This assessment runs under active surveillance and the guidelines are explicit that violations can terminate your attempt. Most of these are fixed in five minutes *before* you start and are unfixable once the clock is running.

### Hard requirements

- **Unstop SmartHire app.** The assessment runs only there. Install and open it well before the window — not at 1:55 PM.
- **Desktop or laptop only.** Phones and tablets are unsupported and you will be forced to switch devices mid-attempt.
- **Working webcam and microphone.** Both are required. Test them in the app first.
- **Fullscreen throughout.** Exiting, switching tabs or minimising "may lead to warnings and eventually termination of your assessment."
- **No external displays.** Physically unplug the second monitor. A connected display can terminate the attempt.

### Things that flag you without you realising

- **Resting your hand on your face.** The guidelines call this out specifically — it can trigger a *"mobile phone detected"* violation. Keep your hands on the keyboard or the desk.
- **Background noise.** Audio is monitored constantly. Other voices, a television, a conversation in the next room, or someone walking in all register as violations. Lock the door and tell your household.
- **Clothing with images or logos.** Explicitly discouraged. Wear something plain.
- **Any of WhatsApp, Discord, Chrome, ChatGPT or similar left open.** Not minimised — **closed**. The guidelines say this causes an *automatic exit* and is flagged. Quit them properly, including anything auto-starting in the background.
- **Screen sharing.** Any detection restricts you from continuing. Close Zoom, Meet, Teams, AnyDesk, OBS.

### The five-minute pre-flight

1. Unplug external monitors. Single screen only.
2. Quit every application except SmartHire. Check the system tray — Discord and Steam hide there.
3. Test webcam and microphone inside the app.
4. Quiet room, door shut, phone in another room, household told.
5. Plain clothing, good lighting on your face, hands off your face.
6. Laptop on mains power, battery saver off, wired internet if you have it, hotspot charged as backup.

**Start early in the window.** It opens 09 Aug 02:00 PM IST and closes 10 Aug 02:00 PM IST, but you must **start by 10 Aug 02:00 PM to get the full hour**. Starting at the last moment leaves no room for a device problem, a webcam failure, or support being slow. Aim to start with many hours of window remaining.
checklist: SmartHire app installed and tested well in advance
External displays physically disconnected
WhatsApp, Discord, Chrome, ChatGPT fully quit, tray included
Webcam and mic tested inside the app
Quiet room secured, phone elsewhere, household warned
Plain clothing, hands off face
Started with hours of the window still left

title: A repeatable procedure for coding under a timer
body:
Under stress you do not rise to the occasion; you fall to your procedure. Do these six things in this order, every time.

**1. Restate the contract.** One line: *input is an array of n ints, output is a single int, n can be 0.* Half of all wrong submissions are correct answers to a slightly different question.

**2. Name the pattern.** Say which one it is out loud. If you cannot name it in 90 seconds, write the brute force — the brute force usually reveals the pattern.

**3. Write the signature and the return first.** Then fill the middle. This stops you writing a function that returns nothing on some path.

**4. Handle degenerate cases at the top.** Empty, single element, all identical. Two lines that cost nothing.

**5. Dry-run on the sample before submitting.** Actually trace it — take sample 1 and walk the state through. Not "it looks right".

**6. Only then submit.** And remember submission is final.

### Patterns worth being able to name instantly

Two pointers · sliding window · prefix sums · hash-map counting · sort-then-scan · binary search on the answer · BFS/DFS on grids and graphs · topological sort · union-find · monotonic stack · heap / top-K · 1D DP · 2D DP · greedy with an exchange argument · bit manipulation.

If you can look at a statement and produce the right name from that list in under two minutes, you will finish both problems. If you cannot, that recognition speed is the single highest-leverage thing to drill in the coding lab.
checklist: Contract restated in one line
Pattern named before coding
Degenerate cases first
Sample dry-run by hand before submit

title: Because the team score is the average
body:
The official brief: *"The team's final score will be calculated based on the average score of all its members."* Every member also takes the assessment **individually** — *"All team members will be able to take the assessments individually."*

**The arithmetic.** In a 3-person team, moving your strongest member from 12/15 to 14/15 lifts the team average by 0.67. Moving your weakest from 6/15 to 10/15 lifts it by 1.33 — **double the return, and far easier**. Marks at the bottom are cheap; marks at the top are expensive.

**With speed marking, this gets sharper.** A member who knows the material but works slowly is losing up to half the available marks on questions they answer *correctly*. That is the cheapest fix in the entire team: it needs no new knowledge, only the habit of submitting the moment they are confident. Drilling submission speed is worth more per hour than drilling any topic.

### The 6-hour crash plan

| Time | What |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:30 | One full mock, cold. Diagnosis, not comfort. |
| 0:30–0:50 | Read the speed-marking and no-going-back sections here. Most of the gap is procedural, not knowledge. |
| 0:50–2:30 | Drill the two weakest topics, Easy and Medium only, **watching the clock on every question**. |
| 2:30–3:30 | Output prediction and complexity questions. Highest-density, most learnable marks in the paper. |
| 3:30–5:00 | Three coding problems: one easy, two medium. Type the solutions yourself, do not read them. |
| 5:00–5:30 | Flashcards, full pass. |
| 5:30–6:00 | Second mock. Compare marks *and* average time per question. |

### The 90-minute panic plan

| Time | What |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:15 | One mock. Diagnosis only. |
| 0:15–0:30 | Read speed marking and no-going-back. This alone is worth marks. |
| 0:30–1:00 | Flashcards, full pass — pure recall moves fastest. |
| 1:00–1:20 | Weakest topic, Easy and Medium only. |
| 1:20–1:30 | Proctoring pre-flight. Set the room up. |

**Team move:** everyone exports their progress from the Progress page and shares the file. Compare topic bars *and* average answer times side by side. The lowest bar in the team is where the group's next hour goes.
checklist: Identify the team's weakest member honestly, today
Everyone runs one mock and exports progress
Compare average answer time, not just accuracy
Slow-but-correct members drill submission speed specifically

title: Round 2: the 45-minute case study
body:
Round 2 is **16 Aug, 12:00 PM – 04:00 PM IST**, individual, 45 minutes in one sitting, one attempt. It is typed prose marked on *analytical thinking, strategic approach, and the ability to derive actionable insights* — that phrasing is from the official brief and it is effectively the rubric.

A completely different skill from Round 1, and the failure modes are logistical as much as intellectual.

**Spend the first 5 minutes not writing.** Read the whole case, all questions, and the data table. Question 4 usually reveals what question 1 was really asking.

**Then allocate by question, not by interest.** Five questions and 40 minutes left is 8 minutes each. Write the split down before you start typing. Running out with the last question blank costs more than any amount of polish on the first.

**Structure every answer identically.** Evaluators skim. One-line verdict, then bullets of evidence, then recommendation, then measurement, then risk. A wall of prose reads as unstructured thinking even when the thinking is good.

**Draft in the answer box, not in another app.** Every extra step is a chance to lose work or run out of time pasting — and tab-switching may well be monitored here too.

**Type speed matters.** At 40 wpm, 8 minutes is 320 words, enough for a strong structured answer. At 20 wpm it is 160 and will read as thin. If you type slowly, use shorter sentences and lean harder on bullets.

**The failure modes that lose the round outright:** not answering the last question; writing everything you know instead of answering what was asked; recommending things with no way to measure them; no numbers anywhere; and generic advice that would survive find-and-replacing the company name.

The full method — the answer skeleton, the frameworks, the quantification patterns and the curveball bank — is in the **Case studio**.
checklist: Read all questions before answering any
Write the per-question minute budget down first
Every answer: verdict, evidence, recommendation, metric, risk
Every recommendation carries a metric and a timeframe
Last question answered even if short
